A developer with extensive WebRTC experience found the launch "a bit lacking." In their view, transcoding and TURN servers (what Twilio seems to offer) aren't the hardest part of WebRTC. Multiplexing is where the complexity lies, and they want a service that makes large-N calls easy, beyond the roughly 10-15 participant limits they hit with Hangouts and their own stack.
On the stated limit of up to 4-way calling over a peer-to-peer mesh, a commenter said: "'up to 4-way calling'... If it said up to 16 that would be more of a game changer."

Another commenter cited CliqMeet as a comparison: it can scale to 100+ participants because it provides an MCU (multiplexing node) service plus auditorium models. Twilio Video's 4-way mesh looked limited by contrast.

Hyperbeam's team found the Agora/Daily/Twilio audio/video calling SDKs "outrageously pricey" for B2C. Even with volume discounts, they would have paid more than $50k/month for about 150k MAU. They built their own simple full-mesh P2P chat instead, which they still use, "although it's far from ideal."

After the announcement that Twilio Video is shutting down, users asked what services companies are migrating to (Zoom? Azure Communication Services?). One said they are currently comparing Zoom vs Daily for a client as a replacement.
